title: Midnight crosscheck pulse — 2026-12-02 shift notes
content:
Purpose
Night shift handover notes + action items after the 00:12–01:10 latency incident affecting model-serving token P95. Intended for next shift (07:00 PST) and engineering owners. Informal notes, TODOs and runbook draft suggestions included.

High-level summary
- Window: 2026-12-02 00:12–01:10 UTC
- Symptom: abrupt rise in model-serving token P95 from ~120ms to 800–1200ms across region-us-west-2; request error rate stayed low (~0.2% spike) but tail latency caused client timeouts and a small number of retries.
- Root suspect: Redis KV cache saturation (connection exhaustion + eviction storm) causing frequent KV misses and forcing runtime to refill KV per-request; observed concurrent Redis clients spikes and slow commands.
- Impact: visible latency SLO breach for ~58 minutes, small fraction of requests timed out; no data loss, no model weight corruption.

Timeline (condensed)
- 00:12 UTC: Alert fired (grafana token_p95 > 600ms) for model-1-v12 in us-west-2. PagerDuty routed to night oncall.
- 00:16 UTC: Confirmed tail latency across both canary routes and primary pools. Dashboards show KV-hit-rate drop from 98% to 27%.
- 00:18 UTC: Began investigating redis metrics (integration: redis-exporter). Connections climbed from ~2.6k -> 6.1k, instantaneous slowlog entries present.
- 00:24 UTC: Applied temporary routing rule to shift 30% of traffic to model-1-v11 (lower memory usage) via traffic-split: /api/v1/route override.
- 00:28 UTC: Increased model-serving replica count (+2 replicas) in region to help absorb CPU spikes (kubectl rollout).
- 00:33 UTC: Restarted redis-read replica in zone-b after noticing one node's client table stuck at ~20k connections.
- 00:40 UTC: Redis eviction storm subsided, KV-hit-rate climbing to 82%, token P95 trending to baseline.
- 01:10 UTC: Alert resolved automatically. Continued monitoring until 02:00 UTC, no regression.

Immediate mitigations performed (commands / quick notes)
- kubectl -n redwood-prod scale deployment/model-serving --replicas=8 (scale from 6 to 8)
- kubectl -n redwood-prod rollout restart deployment/model-serving -l model=model-1-v12 (recycle noisy pods)
- redis-cli -h redis-read-b.us-west-2.info CLIENT LIST | wc -l (confirmed heavy connection table)
- ssh ops@redis-b.zone && redis-cli SLOWLOG GET 20 (reviewed slow commands)
- Updated traffic-split: PATCH /routes/model-1/traffic {'canary': 30, 'primary': 70} (temporary fallback)

Observations / telemetry notes
- KV cache hit-ratio dropped sharply; backend served fallback to scanned weights causing runtime to re-evaluate prefixes more often.
- Redis slowlog showed many repeated GET/EXPIRE patterns for the same prefixes — indicates race where multiple pods concurrently repopulated the same key after eviction.
- One redis replica (redis-read-b) had noticeably elevated tcp_time_wait and a process-level FD leak suspected — after restart the connection count normalized.
- Serving pods displayed CPU spikes coincident with KV-miss surge; memory usage stable.

Detected gaps in runbook/playbook
- No documented play for "redis client-connection exhaustion" -> add granular steps for safely restarting read replicas and verifying client reclamation.
- No explicit recommended traffic-split thresholds for fallback model routing — suggest default values and rollback cadence.
- Missing guidance on when to scale model-serving replicas vs restart redis nodes (order of operations).
- Suggest adding a short diagnostic checklist for oncall to quickly decide: scale / restart / route.

Action items (ordered by priority)
- [P0] JIRA-SRE-4822: Create dedicated runbook section "redis-kv-saturation" (owner: Jon Perez, due: 2026-12-05). Include: diagnostics, restart steps, safe connection drain, verification queries.
- [P0] Ops doc PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/ops-docs/pull/317 — merge runbook edits for temporary traffic-split commands (owner: Maya Li, MR review requested).
- [P1] Add alert: KV-hit-rate < 50% AND token_p95 > 500ms (owner: Aisha Kumar, due: 2026-12-07).
- [P1] Instrument synthetic test: issue small prefix-heavy queries every 30s to detect early KV eviction patterns per-region (owner: infra-test, ticket SRE-4830).
- [P2] Investigate redis-read process FD leak root cause (owner: infra-db, ticket DB-1294).
- [P2] Add autoscale policy: scale-up based on kv_miss_rate or kv_get_latency (owner: platform-engineering).

Follow-ups for next shift
- Verify JIRA-SRE-4822 has initial draft and link it into Confluence (priority: high).
- Confirm redis replica restart did not trigger any persistent cluster imbalance (check replication lag, failover windows).
- Monitor for repeat of distributed eviction within next 48h (add one-time extended retention for related metrics).
- If regression occurs, execute full postmortem; collect heap/dump from a model-serving pod and redis slowlog snapshots.

Runbook draft fragment (to be inserted into Confluence runbook)
- Title: redis-kv-saturation (short play)
- When to use: rapid drop in kv-hit-rate (>30% drop) with coincident token_p95 spike > 500ms for > 5min
- Quick diagnostics:
  1. grafana: verify kv_hit_ratio, redis_connections, redis_slowlog_count, model-serving token_p95
  2. kubectl top pods -n redwood-prod -l app=model-serving
  3. redis-cli INFO replication; redis-cli CLIENT LIST | wc -l
- Immediate mitigation (order):
  a) Temporarily route 20–40% traffic to prior stable model variant (traffic-split)
  b) If cpu spool on serving pods: scale +2 replicas
  c) Identify bad redis replica, safe restart that replica (drain if sentinel enabled)
  d) Monitor kv-hit-rate recovery for 5–10min before undoing traffic-split
- Rollback criteria: token_p95 < 300ms and kv_hit_ratio > 85% for 15min

Notes to oncall (practical tips)
- If you see repeated slowlog entries for identical keys, do NOT restart all redis replicas at once — restart one, validate, then proceed.
- Traffic-split is low-risk but can amplify downstream capacity on older model variants; watch token cost.
- Keep Slack thread #sre-nightwatch pinned with PD incident id PD-INC-2026-1123 for audit.

Unresolved questions
- Why did redis-read-b accumulate so many TCP connections? Need kernel/OS-level observer logs (owner: infra-db).
- Are there any clients not using connection pooling correctly? (owner: dev-platform)

Appendix: useful one-liners
- Check kv hit rate (promql): sum(rate(redis_kv_hits[1m])) / (sum(rate(redis_kv_hits[1m])) + sum(rate(redis_kv_misses[1m])))
- Restart a Redis read replica safely (example): kubectl cordon redis-read-b && kubectl drain redis-read-b --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data && kubectl rollout restart statefulset/redis-read -n infra
- Quick model traffic split: curl -X PATCH https://api.redwood.internal/routes/model-1 -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -d '{"canary_pct":30}'

TL;DR
We saw a KV cache saturation event that increased tail latency. Temporary traffic-split + targeted redis replica restart + replica scale of model-serving pods mitigated the issue. Major next steps: add a focused runbook fragment for redis-kv-saturation (JIRA-SRE-4822), create synthetic early-warning tests, and open infra ticket to investigate connection leak on redis-read-b.

Prepared by: Aisha Kumar (oncall)
Reviewed in-shift: Jon Perez, Maya Li
